title: Re-dating cave art

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Art demonstrates a capacity for human thought this visual expression of a wider symbolic world is a human creation and sets us apart from the rest of the animal kingdom. We know that our symbolic capacity originally developed in Africa, where anatomically modern humans first evolved. Engraved lines on pieces of ochre found in Blombos cave in South Africa show that the use of coloured pigments and geometric patterns appeared at least 100,000 years ago. In addition, shells used for decorative no purposes have been found in deposits of similar age in the extreme north and south of the continent. With figurative art, that is art which represents people, animals or objects, archaeology suggests we are dealing with a much later emergence – perhaps not in our African homeland, but in Australia and Europe.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: We recently carried out a study of cave paintings in northern Spain in order to improve our understanding of cave art in that region. In this study we used a technique which measures the radioactive decay of uranium in order to date the formation of the mineral calcite, which is found in tiny stalactites* on the surface of many of the cave paintings. Although this dating technique has been used by geologists for 50 years, it has only recently been applied to cave art. This is because recent technical advances have reduced the size of samples required to just a few milligrams, allowing us to remove very thin calcite deposits from stalactites which had formed directly on top of fragile paintings.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The oldest dates we obtained came from El Castillo cave, in northern Spain. This artistic treasure house includes a famous panel of hands comprising at least 30 negative hand stencils, made by individuals consciously blowing or spitting pigment at a hand placed on the wall, interspersed by arcs of red dots created with a similar blowing technique. Such hand stencils were previously thought to date back between 23,000 and 28,000 years, but we were able to show that one of the hand stencils in El Castillo was created at least 37,300 years ago, and that one of the red dots in the same area of the cave wall was created over 40,800 years ago. This takes us back into the poorly understood period when in Neanderthal man was disappearing, and in which members of our own species, Homo sapiens, were establishing themselves across Europe for the first time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: So, what did our results indicate? Given this new chronology, we have to remember that something with a minimum age of 40,800 years could actually be 50,000 or even 80,000 years old. Because of this, we can entertain several alternative hypotheses to explain the existence of cave paintings in El Castillo.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the El Castillo paintings are only slightly older than our 40,800-year date, they may have been created by the first 'pioneer' modern humans, Homo sapiens, to arrive in Europe, sometime around 41,500 years ago. Such an early date may even suggest that the tradition of painting caves originated in Europe, as our dates are at least 10,000 years older than those for cave paintings found in Africa. But if so, why did painting first appear in European caves and not those in Africa, when we have evidence of symbolic activity among humans stretching much further back? The answer may be that another human species already existed in Europe, the Neanderthals. Nicholas Conrad, of Tubingen University, says that pioneer groups of Homo sapiens may have found themselves in competition with these indigenous Neanderthals for resources necessary for survival. New social strategies among human groups may have given them the edge. Conrad has suggested that this will have accelerated the rate of cultural innovation, leading very quickly to the appearance of innovations – including musical instruments and figurative art – among modern humans shortly after they arrived in Europe. Our early dates for cave art may show that cave painting – and, presumably, the rituals associated with it – was one of the first of these new symbolic expressions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further hypothesis is possible, however. If the oldest paintings were, in fact, created several thousand years before our date of 40,800, they would predate the arrival of our own species, and so they must have been made by Neanderthals, who we know were present in northern Spain until at least 42,000 years ago. Some scholars automatically reject the notion of Neanderthal art, but there is plenty of evidence of symbolic practices among Neanderthals, such as the deliberate burial of the dead, and the wearing of ornaments.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: So far, our dates do not rule out Neanderthal painters, but nor can we prove they existed. Only further dating of cave art will be able to establish beyond doubt whether Neanderthals really did paint. There are thousands of datable calcite deposits overlying cave paintings, so if we find a conclusive sample, our ongoing work should be able to identify who the painters were. Regardless of whether the artist is Homo sapiens or Homo neanderthalensis, our research is showing that the oldest examples of art are non-figurative, reinforcing the growing recognition that there is a developmental scheme to cave art, with an oldest phase of quite basic patterns made from red pigment. We shall eventually see what this means in evolutionary terms. Turn over ▶

groups.title: A new chronology for cave art: hypotheses and certainties
content: According to Nicholas Conrad, the ability of Homo sapiens to produce art may have been developed through {{23}} for resources with the Neanderthals, who already lived in Europe. It is possible that the cave paintings in El Castillo were one of a number of innovations that Homo sapiens created as a result.

Another possibility is that the first cave paintings were actually produced by Neanderthals. This is supported by their use of {{24}} and the fact that they buried their dead, as well as carrying out other types of symbolic behaviour.

The researchers are still looking for a {{25}} of a calcite deposit that will prove who actually produced the earliest cave paintings. However, they say their findings already show that the earliest known art involved the use of red pigment and took the form of simple {{26}} .

subtitle: Ground-breaking research by Alistair Pike and Paul Pettitt has pushed back the dates for the earliest cave art found in Europe
